title: AP Comparative Government and Politics
summary: Compare institutions, participation and change using evidence from the six course countries.
frameworkNote: 2026–27 structure checked against College Board on 15 October 2026: 5 units. Original VertexED focused lessons and self-check questions sample each unit; they do not replace the full course framework, required materials or teacher review.

modules.title: States, regimes and legitimacy
modules.focus: Distinguish institutions that endure from officeholders who change.
explanation: A state claims authority over a territory and population. A regime is the set of rules governing political power; a government consists of the current officeholders. An election may change the government without changing the regime.

Legitimacy concerns acceptance of authority. Performance, ideology, tradition and participation can contribute to it, while coercion can produce obedience without acceptance. Comparisons need a shared concept and evidence from both cases.

workedExample.prompt: A prime minister loses an election but constitutional rules remain. Classify the change.
steps: The officeholders forming the government change.
The state and basic regime rules can persist through the transfer.

misconception.correction: People may obey because of coercion even when they reject an authority’s right to rule.

questions.prompt: Why is turnout alone insufficient to measure democratic quality?
questions.answer: High turnout can occur with restricted competition or coercion; evidence on participation rights and meaningful alternatives is also needed.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical state expands reliable services. How might that affect legitimacy?
questions.answer: Better services may increase public acceptance of authority, although the effect depends on expectations and other political conditions.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical survey reports trust in institutions, while audit records show widespread failure to carry out their decisions. Explain what each source can establish.
hints: Separate acceptance from implementation.
Avoid treating one measure as a complete judgement.
questions.answer: The survey may illuminate reported legitimacy, subject to its sampling and response conditions. The audit supplies evidence of limited implementation capacity in the audited areas. Neither alone measures both concepts.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical regime changes its leader but preserves its constitution, electoral rules and power structure. Distinguish leadership change from regime change.
hints: Identify what rules changed.
A new officeholder does not automatically create a new political order.
questions.answer: The leadership or government changes, but the supplied rules governing access to and exercise of power persist. The evidence therefore does not establish regime change; a claim of such change would need alterations to those basic rules or practices.

notes.title: Capacity and legitimacy are separate dimensions
paragraphs: Political authority, capacity and legitimacy describe different features of a state. Authority concerns the claimed right to make binding decisions; capacity concerns the ability to implement them; legitimacy concerns acceptance of that right. A government can have substantial enforcement capacity while facing weak voluntary acceptance, or enjoy public support while struggling to deliver policy. Compare these dimensions separately rather than placing every country on one undifferentiated strong–weak scale. Evidence should match the concept: implementation records illuminate capacity, while carefully interpreted public attitudes and patterns of voluntary compliance can inform legitimacy without proving it from obedience alone.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical State A collects taxes reliably but suppresses criticism; State B has broad reported support but cannot consistently deliver rural services. Compare capacity and legitimacy using only the supplied evidence.
steps: Reliable collection indicates capacity in one policy area for A; suppression makes public acceptance harder to infer from compliance.
B’s reported support suggests acceptance, but inconsistent services indicate a capacity limitation.
workedExamples.conclusion: The cases show why administrative ability and public acceptance require separate evidence.

flashcards.back: The ability to implement decisions and provide or enforce policy.
Acceptance of an authority’s right to rule.
No; fear can produce obedience.

flashcards.front: Can high legitimacy coexist with limited capacity?
flashcards.back: Yes; accepted institutions may lack resources or reach.

diagrams.title: Capacity and legitimacy are separate dimensions
diagrams.description: Implementation and acceptance must be measured with different evidence.

modules.title: Executives, legislatures and courts
modules.focus: Trace how formal authority and practical constraints interact.
explanation: In parliamentary systems the executive depends on legislative confidence; in presidential systems executive and legislative mandates are separately established. This difference affects removal, bargaining and responsibility without determining every policy outcome.

Constitutions describe authority, but practice also depends on party control, judicial independence and informal power. Compare the United Kingdom, Mexico and the other course countries with both institutional rules and evidence of operation.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why a parliamentary government may fall after losing a confidence vote.
steps: Its authority to govern relies on support in the legislature.
Loss of that support can trigger replacement or an election under the system’s rules.

misconception.claim: A written constitution proves that courts can constrain leaders.
misconception.correction: Judicial independence depends on appointments, tenure, compliance and political practice.

questions.prompt: How can legislative oversight constrain an executive?
questions.answer: Hearings and investigations can expose implementation failures and support budgetary or legal responses, if the legislature can act independently.

questions.prompt: Why compare judicial appointment rules and actual decisions?
questions.answer: Rules indicate formal independence; decisions and compliance show whether courts can exercise that independence in practice.

questions.prompt: Compare the United Kingdom’s parliamentary executive with Mexico’s presidential executive on the source of their mandates, without predicting which must govern more effectively.
hints: Compare one common institutional dimension.
Mandate structure differs from policy performance.
questions.answer: The UK government relies on parliamentary confidence, while Mexico’s president has a separately established electoral mandate. This changes executive–legislative relationships, but effectiveness also depends on party support, resources and political practice.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical constitution permits legislative investigations, but legislators cannot obtain records or compel testimony. Explain why the formal power may produce weak oversight.
hints: Information is necessary to investigate.
Distinguish written authority from practical tools.
questions.answer: The formal power exists, but lack of access to records and testimony can prevent legislators from discovering or substantiating executive failures. Effective oversight therefore requires operational capacity as well as constitutional authorisation.

notes.title: Coalition support can sustain executive confidence
paragraphs: Institutional comparison asks how one branch can affect another and whether the formal mechanism operates in practice. In the United Kingdom’s parliamentary model, executive survival depends on legislative confidence; in Mexico’s presidential model, the executive has a separately established mandate. This contrast does not imply that presidents face no legal checks or that prime ministers always control their legislatures. Party discipline, coalition bargaining, oversight powers and judicial independence alter the practical balance. Trace a specific mechanism from rule to behaviour and outcome, then identify the evidence needed to test whether it constrained an officeholder in the case being studied.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical parliamentary government holds 48 of 100 seats and relies on a coalition partner with 8. The partner withdraws support. Explain the institutional vulnerability.
steps: The governing party alone lacks a majority of seats, so it may struggle to maintain legislative confidence.
It could seek new support or face replacement under the system’s rules; withdrawal does not by itself establish the exact next event.
workedExamples.conclusion: Coalition arithmetic affects executive survival through the confidence mechanism.

flashcards.front: What connects parliamentary executive survival to the legislature?
flashcards.back: The requirement to retain legislative confidence.
It is established separately from the legislature’s mandate.

flashcards.front: Does formal oversight guarantee effective constraint?
flashcards.back: No; independence, information and enforcement matter.
It affects whether legislators act independently of executive leadership.

diagrams.title: Coalition support can sustain executive confidence
diagrams.description: Losing a partner changes the support available for legislative votes.

modules.title: Political culture and participation
modules.focus: Explain why similar opportunities can produce different participation patterns.
explanation: Political socialisation develops through family, education, media and experience. Shared beliefs may influence participation, but differences within a country prevent its political culture from being reduced to one fixed national personality.

Participation includes voting, protest, petitions and community activity. Resources, repression, trust and perceived effectiveness affect people’s choices. Survey comparisons should use similar questions, samples and dates before attributing differences to culture.

workedExample.prompt: Two surveys report different levels of trust, but one polls only university students.
steps: Identify that the samples represent different populations.
Avoid a national comparison until representative, comparable evidence is available.

misconception.correction: Barriers, boycott, exclusion or distrust can also explain non-voting.

questions.prompt: How might internet censorship affect political participation?
questions.answer: It can restrict access to criticism and make collective action harder, though people may develop alternative networks.

questions.prompt: Why might political trust vary across generations within one country?
questions.answer: Cohorts may have experienced different economic conditions, conflicts or reforms, shaping expectations of institutions.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical country records few public demonstrations but restricts permits and punishes organisers. Explain why demonstration counts alone cannot measure popular satisfaction.
hints: Visible participation depends on opportunity.
Costs can prevent people expressing preferences.
questions.answer: The restrictions raise the risks and coordination costs of protest, so dissatisfied people may remain publicly inactive. Low demonstration counts therefore describe observed action under constraints, not necessarily approval of the government.

questions.prompt: Two hypothetical surveys ask the same approval question, but one is anonymous and the other records names in front of officials. Explain a comparability concern and a remedy.
hints: Perceived consequences can influence answers.
Match conditions as well as wording.
questions.answer: Named responses in front of officials may discourage criticism, producing a response-condition difference. Use comparable confidential methods and representative samples before attributing the contrast solely to political attitudes.

notes.title: Organisation can convert a grievance into participation
paragraphs: Collective political action depends on both motivation and the ability to coordinate. A shared grievance does not automatically produce a protest because participants may face costs while hoping others act for them. Organisations, communication networks and selective benefits can reduce this collective-action problem. Restrictions on association can raise coordination costs, while repression can deter participation or sometimes generate further opposition; the outcome requires evidence. Survey responses also depend on whether people feel safe expressing disagreement. Compare participation opportunities and measurement conditions before interpreting a low protest count or a high approval figure as a complete account of political culture.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical residents all want cleaner water, but each expects others to attend a costly council meeting. A neighbourhood group arranges transport and speaking roles. Explain the change.
steps: Initially, the public benefit and individual participation costs create an incentive to rely on others.
Organisation reduces costs and coordinates contributions, making participation easier.
workedExamples.conclusion: Shared grievances become more likely to generate collective action when coordination barriers fall.

flashcards.back: People may avoid individual costs while hoping to share benefits from others’ action.
They coordinate people and reduce participation costs.

flashcards.front: Does low protest necessarily mean satisfaction?
flashcards.back: No; barriers or repression may suppress visible activity.

flashcards.front: Why consider safety in political surveys?
flashcards.back: Fear can affect willingness to report dissent.

modules.title: Electoral rules and organised interests
modules.focus: Connect seat allocation to representation and strategy.
explanation: Plurality elections award a seat to the candidate with the most votes in a district. Proportional systems translate party votes into seats more proportionally, subject to thresholds and design. Neither rule alone describes an entire political system.

Political parties seek office, while interest groups seek influence over decisions. Civil society organisations may express independent interests; state-controlled organisations can instead channel participation within limits set by authorities.

workedExample.prompt: In one plurality district, parties receive 42%, 35% and 23%. Who wins?
steps: The party with 42% receives the seat because it has the largest vote share.
It does not need an absolute majority under this rule.

misconception.claim: Plurality and majority mean the same thing.
misconception.correction: Plurality means the largest share; a majority exceeds half.

questions.prompt: Why can a small party win more representation under proportional allocation?
questions.answer: Its votes can contribute to seats across a wider area instead of needing first place in individual districts, subject to thresholds.

questions.prompt: How does an independent trade union differ from a government-controlled one?
questions.answer: An independent union can formulate members’ demands outside state direction; government control can limit what demands and actions are permitted.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical party X wins 40% in each of five two-party plurality districts while Y wins 60% in each. Find X’s seats and explain the result despite its substantial support.
questions.hint: Seats are awarded district by district.
hints: Seats are awarded district by district.
Second place everywhere earns no seats under this rule.
questions.answer: X wins zero of five seats because Y has the larger share in every district. X’s 40% overall vote share does not become proportional seats in this single-member plurality model.

questions.prompt: Compare a party with regionally concentrated support and one with the same total votes spread evenly across UK-style single-member plurality districts. Explain a possible representation difference.
questions.hint: Ask where each party can finish first.
hints: Ask where each party can finish first.
Do not assume total votes alone determine seats.
questions.answer: The concentrated party may win pluralities in its strong region, while the dispersed party may finish second or lower everywhere. Thus equal total support can produce unequal seats, although actual results depend on opponents and district boundaries.

notes.title: District outcomes can diverge from total vote share
paragraphs: Electoral geography can produce different seat outcomes from the same overall vote share. Under single-member plurality rules, geographically concentrated support may win districts while equally numerous dispersed supporters win none. The UK House of Commons provides a course example of district plurality elections, where regional concentration can matter for smaller parties. Proportional rules reduce some vote–seat disparities but thresholds and district magnitude still affect representation. Separate an electoral rule from the broader political context: competitive rights, party organisation and access to campaigning determine whether voters can use that rule meaningfully. Seat arithmetic alone cannot establish democratic quality.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical three-district plurality election: party A wins 60%, 60% and 20%; party B receives the remainder. Each district has equal turnout. Find A’s vote share and seats.
steps: A’s overall share is (60 + 60 + 20)/3 = 46⅔%.
A wins the first two districts and therefore 2 of 3 seats.
workedExamples.conclusion: A receives a seat majority without an overall vote majority because district victories determine seats.

flashcards.back: More votes than any other candidate in the relevant district.

flashcards.front: Why can concentrated support help a small party?
flashcards.back: It can win local pluralities instead of finishing behind everywhere.
The number of seats elected in a district.

flashcards.front: Does proportional representation guarantee unrestricted competition?
flashcards.back: No; political rights and implementation also matter.

diagrams.title: District outcomes can diverge from total vote share
diagrams.description: Equal-turnout district results determine seats separately.

edges.label: aggregate seats and votes by different rules

modules.title: Development, reform and political change
modules.focus: Separate economic measures from political processes.
explanation: Economic growth measures increased output, while development can include health, education and distribution. Market liberalisation changes economic allocation; democratisation changes access to political power. One can occur without the other.

Global trade, resource dependence and policy reforms can create winners and losers. To explain change, identify a mechanism such as revenue dependence, new social groups or external pressure, then test it against evidence rather than assuming a universal sequence.

workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical country privatises firms but restricts opposition parties.
steps: Privatisation can represent economic liberalisation.
Restricted political competition means that this change alone does not establish democratisation.

misconception.claim: Rising GDP proves equal improvement for everyone.
misconception.correction: An average can increase while inequality or regional disadvantages persist.

questions.prompt: Why might dependence on one exported commodity make state revenue unstable?
questions.answer: A price decline reduces export earnings and tax or royalty receipts, limiting spending even if production changes little.

questions.prompt: What would help evaluate whether growth improved development?
questions.answer: Evidence on health, education, poverty and distribution would show whether gains reached people and improved capabilities.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical public revenue is 40 export-tax units and 60 other units. Export-tax receipts fall by one-quarter. Find the new total and explain why total revenue does not fall by 25%.
questions.hint: Apply the change only to the affected component.
hints: Apply the change only to the affected component.
Then recombine the unchanged component.
questions.answer: Export-tax receipts fall by 10 to 30 units, giving total revenue of 90. The overall decline is 10%, because only 40% of initial revenue experienced the 25% fall.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical government privatises a utility but keeps opposition parties restricted. Explain what reform is demonstrated and what political claim remains unsupported.
questions.hint: Identify the allocation or ownership change.
hints: Identify the allocation or ownership change.
Assess political competition separately.
questions.answer: Privatisation changes ownership and may form part of economic liberalisation. It does not establish democratisation because the supplied restrictions still limit political competition; evidence of broader rights and meaningful access to power would be needed.

notes.title: A revenue shock can alter policy choices
paragraphs: Political and economic reforms can affect accountability through different mechanisms. Tax-financed spending may create incentives for citizens to demand information about public funds, while large external resource revenues can reduce some governments’ immediate dependence on broad domestic taxation. This is a conditional argument, not a law that resource wealth produces one regime type. Institutions, ownership, transparency and distribution shape how revenue is used. Economic liberalisation also changes who gains income and influence, but those changes do not automatically broaden political rights. A strong comparison identifies the intervening mechanism and tests it with revenue and institutional evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical state receives 70 of 100 revenue units from one export royalty. The royalty falls by half while other revenue is unchanged. Find the new total and a political implication.
steps: Royalty revenue falls from 70 to 35; other revenue remains 30.
Total revenue becomes 65, a 35% decline.
workedExamples.conclusion: The shortfall may create pressure to cut spending, borrow or raise taxes, with different accountability consequences.

flashcards.back: No; economic allocation and political access are distinct.

flashcards.front: Why can concentrated export revenue create vulnerability?
flashcards.back: A shock to one commodity can strongly reduce public income.
The process linking a proposed cause to its outcome.

flashcards.front: Does resource dependence determine regime type by itself?
flashcards.back: No; institutions and political choices also matter.
